title: What a Price Does to a Thing

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the twenty-first of November, twenty twenty-six. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
It's the weekend edition, so we start with a watch. A nineteen fifty-two Patek Philippe, off the market for thirty-seven years, goes under the hammer in Hong Kong today.
[excited] And the rabbit hole is Go — the board game — where the best clamshell stones cost eleven million yen a set.
For stones.
[laughs] For stones. And if you're driving the Great Ocean Road this summer, the Twelve Apostles now take booked arrival slots.
All of that later. The lead is heavier. The World Court has found a state guilty of genocide — for the first time.
No spine this weekend. A straight book. Let's go to The Hague.

Thursday, the nineteenth of November. The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, during the army's twenty seventeen "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine State.
And "first time" means what, exactly?
In the court's eighty years, it has never found a state itself guilty of the crime. [pause] Not merely of failing to stop it.
[thoughtful] Because intent is the hard part.
Intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part. In two thousand and seven the court found Serbia had failed to prevent Srebrenica — but had not committed genocide.
So what was different this time?
The court said the "only reasonable inference" was intent. It counted at least ten thousand Rohingya killed, and one thousand eight hundred and thirty-four rapes.
[sighs] And the infants.
The murder of infants, it said, "supports the inference" of intent to prevent births.
Nearly four hundred villages razed. Many bulldozed and built over with security posts. Some seven hundred thousand people fled to Bangladesh.
President Yuji Iwasawa read for three hours. The core finding passed nine votes to six.
Who were the six?
Vice-President Julia Sebutinde. Judges Tomka, Abraham and Nolte. Xue Hanqin of China. And Myanmar's own ad hoc judge, Claus Kress.
And in the majority, The Gambia's ad hoc judge, Navi Pillay — this year's Nobel Peace laureate. The American judge, Sarah Cleveland, voted with her.
Myanmar must compensate the Rohingya, allow their return, and report back within two years. It was cleared, fourteen to one, of inciting genocide. There is no appeal.
How did Naypyitaw take it?
[deadpan] The spokesperson, Khaing Khaing Soe, said: "Nine agreed with this decision. Six disagreed… it is not fair." Then she cited Trump, Xi and Putin on international courts.
And Min Aung Hlaing spent the day of the ruling receiving the secretary-general of BIMSTEC, the Bay of Bengal grouping. The state papers led on that.
Beijing objected the next day. Guo Jiakun, at the foreign ministry, said China has "concerns regarding such issues as ultra vires jurisdiction and overreach in interpretation".
And when he was asked about the Chinese judge's votes?
Judges "serve in their individual capacity and perform their duties independently".
[wry] Of course they do. The Guardian's view is: read it through Washington.

Because South Africa's Gaza case against Israel is pending, and this reasoning on intent is why Washington watched. Judges had sought advice on shielding their assets from American sanctions. And Mike Waltz, the American envoy to the United Nations, warned he would not let "globalist, faux judges" weaponise the law.

The rights groups heard something else. Wai Wai Nu, of the Women's Peace Network, said it "brings hope to millions of Rohingya". António Guterres called it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims".
Now the sceptic box. A genocide ruling nobody can enforce.
[curious] What happens if Myanmar simply ignores it?

The Gambia's only recourse is the Security Council. Which has never used that power. And where China, Russia and America hold vetoes — the same three whose Shenzhen declaration told courts not to "abuse" jurisdiction.
Ah. Yesterday's story, coming back around.
Six of fifteen judges dissented. Min Aung Hlaing now rules as president. And more than a million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh.
[thoughtful] So the court can order compensation…
…but it cannot collect it.
Okay. Money. [exhales] It was a week.
The S and P five hundred fell three point seven per cent on Friday, to six thousand nine hundred and ten. Its seventh straight daily loss.
[wry] Which makes it, officially, a correction.
More than ten per cent below the record. Down almost nine per cent on the week — the worst since the tariff shock of April twenty twenty-five. The Nasdaq is now down for the year.
And the new part is where the money went.
Into government bonds. When a bond is bought, its yield — the interest a new buyer earns — falls. The ten-year Treasury went from five point oh four to four point nine two per cent.
What about gold? Isn't that the classic hiding place?
[deadpan] Not this week. Gold fell two point seven eight per cent, to three thousand five hundred and twenty-four dollars. Investors sold what they could to raise dollars.
And bitcoin?
Fifty-eight thousand one hundred and eighty-eight dollars. Down twenty-eight per cent in four weeks.
[whispers] Ouch.
And markets still expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates on the ninth of December. Governor Lisa Cook said on Friday that waiting "risks getting behind the curve".
So after all that — are shares cheap now?
Depends on the ruler. FactSet's forward measure, price over next year's expected profit, fell to seventeen point one. That's below its ten-year average.
Cheap-ish, then.

Robert Shiller's measure, which looks back ten years, read thirty-seven point eight six. More than twice its long-run median. Only the dot-com peak, in December nineteen ninety-nine, ever topped August's reading.
[curious] So which ruler is right?

The gap between them is a bet on profit margins. Turn each one upside down into an earnings yield: five point eight per cent on the forward view, two point six on Shiller's. A ten-year inflation-protected Treasury pays two point seven seven.
[skeptical] So on Shiller's arithmetic you're paid less than nothing for owning shares.
Exactly. The Fed's own stability report found valuations "well above" the historical median. And "very oversold" — Deutsche Bank's phrase on Friday — is not the same as cheap.
For the reader's own fund, the all-world V W R A?

Net asset value of one hundred and seventy-eight dollars eighty-one at the nineteenth, down one point six per cent. Sixty-two point eight three per cent American. The desk's lean is lower; a net asset value above one hundred and eighty dollars on the twenty-seventh proves it wrong.
And the PIMCO income fund?

The Singapore-dollar hedged class was down twelve hundredths of a per cent on the week. Lean: up a little, as falling yields outweigh wider spreads. The standing call is still a real-rate shock. And all of that is explanation, not advice.
Singapore now. Lawrence Wong was in Shenzhen.

He met Xi Jinping on Friday, for twenty-five minutes. They agreed to start negotiating a fourth version of the free-trade agreement — the "four point oh" upgrade — covering the digital economy and government procurement.
Why should anyone care on a Saturday morning?

[wry] Nothing changes at the checkout this weekend. But China is Singapore's biggest goods partner: one hundred and sixty-two point nine billion dollars of trade last year, eleven point seven per cent of the total.
And the timeline?
No timetable, no text. The last upgrade took four years. And procurement is harder — China has been only an observer to the World Trade Organization's procurement pact since two thousand and two.
Two quick ones. The October exports figure we held is now settled.

Seasonally adjusted, October's non-oil domestic exports rose fourteen point two per cent on September. And if you were born in nineteen seventy-six or earlier, the C P F top-up — five hundred to fifteen hundred dollars — lands by the eighth of December, automatically.
And it's Saturday, which means — [laughs] the Scoreboard.
Forty-five calls came due. Twenty right, fifteen wrong, one push, nine unsettled.
Go on. The worst miss.
Four separate issues said October's exports would grow more slowly than September's sixty-eight per cent. They grew seventy-nine point eight.
[chuckles] Four times.
Four times. And twice we said Anthropic would price inside a range. It priced at eighty-three dollars — above it.
Humility, with footnotes. Technology — and it's Nvidia again.

Down fourteen per cent on Friday, closing at one hundred and twenty-five dollars fifty-three. A seventh straight weekly fall, the longest run since two thousand and eight. CNBC puts the seven-week loss at about two point six trillion dollars.
But the business isn't collapsing?
Third-quarter revenue was one hundred and fifteen point eight billion dollars, up one hundred and three per cent. Sales are still doubling.
So what are investors pricing?

[deadpan] The people. Jensen Huang resigned on the twelfth of November. The new board chair, Harvey Jones, says he left after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct". The finance chief, Colette Kress, is interim chief executive. No permanent one named.
And now there's an accounting report.
A Reuters report that the S E C is examining potential accounting issues. It rests on unnamed sources, the desk did not read it at source, and no finding has been made.
But the sceptic says don't panic.

Eight point four times next year's earnings, against twenty-nine for A M D. And here's the oddity. Nvidia is among the companies that agreed to buy Anthropic stock at the eighty-three-dollar offer price. That stake is about seven per cent above cost — while Nvidia's own shares have lost almost half.
So the chipmaker is now a cheaper bet on A I than one of its own customers.
Nvidia also turns up on the Home Lab page. Its Windows drivers.
[curious] The chatty driver.

A display service keeps rewriting one log file all day, even when the machine is idle. In one test on the fourth-of-November driver, five hundred and fifteen megabytes in five idle minutes. On the October driver, under two.
And that matters because solid-state drives wear out a little with every write.

One owner reported about thirty gigabytes an hour. At that rate a machine writes some seven hundred and twenty gigabytes a day. Most of a one-terabyte drive. But the thirty is one owner's. Windows counts what a program asks to write, not what reaches the chips; Wccftech's own idle machine saw about five gigabytes an hour. The reported cure is rolling back to driver six two one point oh one. Nvidia hadn't acknowledged it by Friday.
Okay, something joyful. The Kit.
Teenage Engineering's first CD player, the E P slash B C one. Three hundred and twenty-nine US dollars.
[excited] And the disc spins on top. In plain sight. It looks more like a record player.
A dial slows or speeds the music from fifty to one hundred and fifty per cent. It detects tempo, streams over Bluetooth and runs on a battery.
And it reads CD indexes — points inside a single track, like the movements of a symphony. Almost no modern player finds those. One Hacker News commenter was thrilled for his classical discs.
The sceptic: no X L R sockets, no R C A out either. One commenter called the design "dang dangerous" — he's had so many CDs blow up in his drive. And the desk found no Singapore price or stockist.
[laughs] Noted. And the Atelier did door handles.

Graded ones. HOPPE's stainless Amsterdam lever prints its test grade: two hundred thousand turns, and two hundred and forty hours of salt spray — the grade written for "maritime air", which is exactly what Singapore's coastal air asks for. It sits in a price class of sixty-one to eighty euros, though that's from a search snippet only.
And the lovely brass ones?
Croft's unlacquered solid-brass Crest lever, two hundred and fifty-nine pounds twenty-five a pair. It prints no grade at all. None of the brass houses did.
[thoughtful] So past a solid body and a sprung rose —
— money buys the casting and the finish.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Even on a weekend.
Especially on a weekend. [laughs] Go. Weiqi in China, baduk in Korea, igo in Japan. More than two thousand five hundred years old — the oldest board game still played.
Remind me of the rules.

Black and white stones on the crossings of a nineteen-by-nineteen grid. You take turns, each trying to wall off more of the board. Surround a stone or a group completely and you capture it. That's nearly all of it.
And a lot of people outside East Asia fell in because of a machine.
March twenty sixteen. Google's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul. Then AlphaGo Zero, taught only by playing itself, beat AlphaGo a hundred games to nothing.
[deadpan] Humbling.
But! This July the world number one, Shin Jin-seo, took on the free engine KataGo with two handicap stones — worth about eighteen points — and won the series two to one.
The decider by eleven and a half points, after two hundred and twenty-one moves. The purse was two hundred and fifty million won and a Genesis G ninety.
And his line afterwards is lovely. "I asked for favorable conditions."
[chuckles] At least he's honest. How many people actually play?

A twenty sixteen survey counted more than forty-six million who know the game and over twenty million current players. The Singapore Weiqi Association says local players grew from about a hundred to "over two hundred thousand".
Here's the part that struck me. The price of the A I tutor is sameness.

Yes. Shin's nickname is "Shintelligence", for how closely he plays like the machine. One study found his moves matched the A I's thirty-seven point five per cent of the time, against an average of twenty-eight point five.
And Korea's national coach reckons an elite player loses about point three of a point to the strongest A I on every move. Shin cut that to point two.
Now — the gear. This is where you'll groan.
I'm braced.
The board, the goban, is best cut from kaya — Japanese Torreya. A protected tree, felled only once it has died. The finest come from trees up to seven hundred years old.
And the cheaper version?
"Shin-kaya". New kaya. Which is actually North American spruce that looks the part.
[amused] Very diplomatic name.

Grain sets the price. Straight grain, masame, is prized. Straight on top and bottom, tenchi-masa, is the summit. The Nihon Ki-in's twenty nineteen catalogue priced a six-sun kaya floor board at one point five to five million yen.
And the stones.
Black is slate from Kumano. White was clamshell from Hyuga — now "nearly extinct" — so almost all shell comes from Baja California. They're graded by the stripes: snow, above moon, above practical.
And the eleven million.

Kurokigoishiten's flawless Premium snow sets run from one hundred and fifty-eight thousand four hundred yen, at seven and a half millimetres thick, to eleven million and eighty-eight thousand yen at fourteen point three.
[gasps] Same grade? Same diameter?
Same grade, same diameter. Six point eight millimetres more shell. [drawn out] Seventy times the price.
[deadpan] And thicker shell plays no better.
It does not. That's the sceptic box. Oh — and black stones are cut point three of a millimetre wider, because black looks smaller next to white.
[laughs] Okay, that's genuinely good.
The sensible first serious buy is Kurokigoishiten's own set — a shin-kaya board, clamshell stones, chestnut bowls — for fifty-nine thousand nine hundred yen.
And for a total beginner here?

Learn on the small nine-by-nine board, free, on O G S or the mobile GoQuest. Then the Singapore Weiqi Association's adult class: eight weekly lessons at Bishan Community Club, two hundred and eighty dollars. Thirty off if you're over sixty.
Give me some vocabulary to bluff with.
Atari — one move from capture. Sente — a move that forces a reply. And my favourite, aji. "Taste." The latent trouble you leave behind.
[wry] I leave aji everywhere.
You really do. But the case against is real. A I has made the opening an answer key — the first fifty moves often match its picks. Lee Sedol says copy from one and "that's no longer art."
And Ke Jie?
"Very tiring and painful to watch."
Back up to the surface, and that watch.
Lot nine five eight. The last lot of this morning's eleven o'clock session at Phillips, in West Kowloon.
A nineteen fifty-two Patek Philippe reference twenty-four ninety-nine, first series, in yellow gold. A perpetual calendar chronograph.
[curious] Which does what, for the rest of us?
Shows day, date, month and moon phase, knows how long each month runs, and adds a stopwatch. S J X calls it "once the most complicated wristwatch in serial production". About ten were made a year.
It last sold in public in nineteen eighty-nine. The case, by Edouard Wenger, "has never been polished".
But "the dial has likely seen some love". That's the condition question bidders will price.
And the estimate?

Twelve to twenty-four million Hong Kong dollars — about one point five four to three point oh eight million US. Its closest yellow-gold cousins made fifteen point four, and about eighteen point seven, million Hong Kong dollars. May's eighty point three seven million record was for pink gold. Meridian expects a result inside the estimate, below twenty million. The hammer falls after this issue closes.
So the next issue prints it. And grades us.
The family desk, for parents of teenagers. Stony Brook metered the phones of two hundred and eighteen American thirteen-to-eighteen-year-olds.
Metered, not asked. Which matters, because teenagers guess their own screen time badly.
Each extra hour of phone use between eleven at night and six in the morning went with about twenty-six minutes less sleep. An extra hour of night-time social media, about forty-four.
And it's sharper in girls. Each extra evening hour went with falling asleep eighty-two minutes later.
Don't be alarmist, though. It's one snapshot. A child who can't sleep may pick up the phone, not the reverse. And the eighty-two is a per-hour slope from about a hundred and nine girls.
[warmly] The lead author's advice is simple. Charge the phone in another room.
General guidance, not medical advice. And finally, Melbourne. Since the sixteenth of October, the Twelve Apostles can only be visited on a booked arrival time.
A new visitor centre, one hundred and twenty-six million Australian dollars. Free until April twenty twenty-seven, then a fee of a size nobody has announced.
The desk's advice: two nights, not one day. Sleep at Lorne, then Port Campbell, and take dawn at the stacks.
And the sceptic box is gleeful. There were never twelve, one fell in two thousand and five, and Loch Ard Gorge — unbooked — is the better photograph.
[deadpan] Book the stacks. Photograph the gorge.
[thoughtful] Which brings us to the Undercurrent. Let's slow down for this one.
Amity Scarth is twenty-two. She wears a rabbit-fur vest to dinner and a fox-fur scarf to parties.
[amused] And she'll tell anyone who asks where both animals died.
Her rules are what Australians have started calling feral fur. The animal must be a pest. Killed humanely. Tanned and sewn in Australia.

Her vest was made by Heidi Beynon — a former art and woodwork teacher turned goat farmer, who began by tanning the hides of goats she killed for meat… and then found the deer and fox hunters. It's her full-time trade now.
"Fur is designed to last a really long time," Scarth told the A B C.
[warmly] And it is a clean answer to the buyer's question. Did this animal die for my vanity? No. The fox was going to die anyway.
The essay grants that. It calls feral fur a sound ethic — and a risky economics. Because a pest with a price acquires a constituency.
[pause] A harvester wants a crop next year. An eradicator wants there to be no next year.
New Zealand has run this experiment for almost two centuries. Possums were shipped from Australia in eighteen thirty-seven, expressly to establish a fur trade.
And researchers followed the commercial trappers. A trapper starts a line where half to seven in ten traps hold a possum each night… and pulls out at about a quarter.
Because below that he loses money. And that is roughly where conservation starts to pay.
So the line is rested for about three years, while the possums recover. [sighs] A managed herd. Not a falling one.

Victoria has the same shape with deer. Perhaps more than a million of them. Hunting worth more than two hundred and one million Australian dollars a year, by the shooters' association's account. And the state still pays professionals to cull — and is paying two hundred thousand dollars just to count them again.
And the purest case of all is Hanoi, in nineteen oh two.
The French administration paid a cent for each rat tail. Officials soon saw tailless rats in the streets. [deadpan] Health inspectors found rat farms on the city's edge.
[chuckles] Pay for the evidence of a kill, and people learn to produce the evidence.

The sceptic says this trade is far too small to matter. A stall and a part-time hand. And New Zealand's researchers prescribed subsidy, not prohibition — pay trappers to keep working below the line where fur stops paying.
So the honest line isn't real against faux. Or farmed against wild.
[thoughtful] It's between a pelt that's a by-product of control somebody else has paid for… and a pelt whose price decides how many animals die.

[pause] Aldo Leopold, on the contents page this week. "We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect."
Scarth is right that fur is made to last.
[warmly] The question her vest raises is whether the fox should.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-nine pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
